prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets, with endogenous prices and unobserved product characteristics, which made empirical industrial organisation a quantitative basis for analysing market power, mergers and regulation

statement.case_for: My configuration changed. In round 1 I preferred B027 (Kiyotaki and Moore) and ranked B005 eighth in my opening. For this final discussion I tried to apply the chair's single test to all four leading candidates: did the work change what can be credibly known, has it been validated in use or in evidence, is the credit attributable to a small set of people, and does it add something beyond a recent prize? B027 does best on conceptual originality and attribution. It does less well on direct validation and on distinctness from the 2022 prize, which several colleagues, and I myself, flagged as the weakest parts of the case. B005 passes all four parts of the test on the evidence in the files. The Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes random-coefficients framework made it possible to estimate substitution patterns, market power and merger effects from market data with endogenous prices. Colleagues report three decades of use in merger review, antitrust, regulation, trade, health and environmental work. Pakes also anchors the dynamic-industry strand. My opening objection was diffuse attribution, and it applied to the seven-name ballot list, not to the citation as now framed. Once the citation rests on the demand-estimation core, the three names map onto one jointly authored contribution. My second objection was methods versus discovery. I no longer think that distinction should count against a tool that changed what can be answered with data, and I would apply the same standard to every candidate. I am not moving because five colleagues prefer B005. Support counts say nothing about merit. I moved because the attribution argument and the validated-use argument, once stated, answered my two specific objections better than I had expected. I also cannot exclude that my macro background made B027 look better to me than the common test supports.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that B005 is a methods and measurement prize with no single headline finding, and the Committee might reasonably rank a conceptual mechanism such as B027 above it. Estimates from BLP-type models depend on instruments, functional form and equilibrium assumptions, so the citation must not suggest settled empirical results. The three-name cap excludes Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, who have real claims to the wider empirical-IO tradition and the dynamic strand. I am not an IO specialist and have not verified the robustness and replication claims in the colleagues' openings. If the Committee thinks conceptual originality should outweigh breadth of validated use, B027 remains the better candidate on that criterion and is my first alternative.

responses.point: Andersson answered my round-1 objections to B005. He accepts that the seven-name ballot credit set is diffuse but argues the three-person core is not. He treats implementation sensitivity as evidence of long scrutiny, and he asks that a method be judged by whether it changed what can be credibly learned about welfare and policy questions. He also said he would not call B005 clearly stronger than B027.
responses.response: Your test is the one I now use, and applied to B005 it moves me. The core attribution is clear once the citation is tied to the demand-estimation framework. I accept that sensitivity to implementation limits how the estimates should be used. It does not undermine the originality of the method. I also agree that B005 is not clearly stronger than B027 on conceptual originality. Our difference is about which criterion should decide the margin, and I now put validated, policy-relevant use ahead of originality. I would not call the choice obvious, and it rests partly on claims about use that I have not verified independently.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B027 and acknowledges that its empirical standing is weaker than B005's documented use. He argues that the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism differs from the 2022 bank-run and intermediation work, and he would not add Gertler or Gilchrist.
responses.response: I agree with you on the two-name attribution, on leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist, and on the mechanisms being different from the 2022 work. I am moving anyway, and you should not read it as independent evidence against B027, since you and I share a long co-authorship and an institution. I now think the weaker validation that you yourself concede counts for more than I gave it in round 1, and that overlap with a recent prize is a risk the Committee will raise even if it is answerable. I would put B027 first among the alternatives. If colleagues weigh conceptual originality above breadth of validated use, I would not resist that outcome.

responses.point: Friberg revised his third name from Bresnahan to Levinsohn. He argues that a demand-estimation citation should credit all three authors of the BLP paper, and that the diffuseness problem disappears once the citation is narrowed to demand and competition in differentiated-product markets.
responses.response: This is the argument that resolved my attribution concern, and it is why my proposed laureates are Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. I note that you have a field interest in this prize, which you disclosed, so I weigh the point on its reasoning, not on your standing. The reasoning holds because the citation and the credit set are matched to one identifiable contribution. I would want the citation wording to state that scope explicitly. If the Committee wanted to reward Bresnahan's market-power tradition, that would need a different, broader citation and not a substitution here.

responses.point: Enflo moved from B025 to B005 partly because of my round-1 point about Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum. She disagreed with my low ranking of B005 and said implementation sensitivity limits use but not originality.
responses.response: I think you are right on the last point and I have revised my ranking accordingly. Implementation sensitivity is a limit on how the estimates are used, not a measure of the originality of the method. I still hold that the uncredited parallel contribution to B025 is a real problem for that ballot, and it is part of why I keep B025 out of my alternatives. I accept your point that a prize on measurement tools can be a discovery. I would add that the citation should state plainly that it rewards a method.

responses.point: Strömberg argues that Levinsohn should stay in a demand-estimation citation because dropping one author of BLP breaks the cleanest attribution. He also withdrew his opening proposal to add Gertler to B027, and he rates B014 as strong but with weaker identification than the BLP estimators.
responses.response: I agree on keeping Levinsohn. Your withdrawal of Gertler from B027 also removes the one attribution dispute I had on that ballot, so my alternative B027 stays at two names, Kiyotaki and Moore. I accept your concern about identification on B014 and I treat that as a reason it is not among my alternatives. I read your caution about overstating settled empirical knowledge as applying to my own citation, so the wording is on methods and not on findings.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee wants a narrow demand-estimation citation, as I propose, or a wider empirical-IO citation that would bring in Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard or Levin and so change the laureate set.

Whether conceptual originality (B027) should outweigh breadth of validated use (B005) on the margin. I weigh it that way now, but I have not verified the claims about use, replication or prior prizes in the files.
How much BLP implementation sensitivity should count against a methods contribution, given that I am not an IO specialist.
Whether the 2022 prize overlap with B027 and the 2024 overlap with B014 should count as a bar or as a weight, and whether my current view of B027's distinctness is too generous or too severe.
Whether, if B005 fails to gather enough support, the Committee would find B027 or B030 (with Dorn in place of Katz, as I said in round 1) the better fallback.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Berry, Levinsohn or Pakes is apparent from my profile, nor to Kiyotaki, Moore or the other credited names on my alternatives. My profile does list Per Krusell (secretary) as a frequent co-author and John Hassler (chair) as a co-author, with IIES colleagueship with both. Krusell prefers B027 and Hassler prefers B014, so my move away from B027 and my positions on B005 should not be read as agreement or disagreement independent of those ties. I am also a long-running co-author of Peter Klenow (B046, not in my configuration or alternatives). My collaborators Aghion, Bergeaud, Li, Ngai and others do not appear among the shortlisted credited names. My field, macroeconomics, is closer to B027 and B036 than to B005. I disclose these facts and do not adjudicate them.
